# How did coordinated disclosure fail, and what does AI-assisted discovery change?

B
The answer in thirty seconds

A bug class seen and shelved in 2024 was turned into working exploits by three AI-assisted teams within three weeks in August 2026. The disclosure leaked 22.5 hours early. Agencies split on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

Read the site as Blake →

What this incident says about coordinated disclosure once models can find bugs, and once a leak can become a proof of concept faster than a patch can ship. The claims below are the evidence; the reading is the site's.

## What to decide or do
- The window between leak and release was 22.5 hours and the window between first honeypot hit and release was four days. Both are shorter than the two months the fix took.
- Three AI-assisted teams converged on a bug class seen and shelved in 2024. The constraint that failed in 2024 was proving exploitability, and that is what models now appear to lower the cost of.
- The defensive side moved early too: WAF rules 9 hours ahead, images 6 hours ahead (against the embargo), agencies within the hour. The system is faster in both directions.
- The public numbers were not produced for decision-making and should not be used for it; the one agency that counted got about 6,000 in a country of 1.9 million people.
- Agencies diverged on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post. No copy of that post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The BBC's list (parts of Wikipedia, Edinburgh council, French government services, the University of Geneva, the BBC itself) has not been captured from any of those organisations. Latvia's geo-blocking is the one documented case, from the agency itself.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

# How did coordinated disclosure fail, and what does AI-assisted discovery change?

B
The answer in thirty seconds

A bug class seen and shelved in 2024 was turned into working exploits by three AI-assisted teams within three weeks in August 2026. The disclosure leaked 22.5 hours early. Agencies split on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

Read the site as Blake →

What this incident says about coordinated disclosure once models can find bugs, and once a leak can become a proof of concept faster than a patch can ship. The claims below are the evidence; the reading is the site's.

## What to decide or do
- The window between leak and release was 22.5 hours and the window between first honeypot hit and release was four days. Both are shorter than the two months the fix took.
- Three AI-assisted teams converged on a bug class seen and shelved in 2024. The constraint that failed in 2024 was proving exploitability, and that is what models now appear to lower the cost of.
- The defensive side moved early too: WAF rules 9 hours ahead, images 6 hours ahead (against the embargo), agencies within the hour. The system is faster in both directions.
- The public numbers were not produced for decision-making and should not be used for it; the one agency that counted got about 6,000 in a country of 1.9 million people.
- Agencies diverged on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

B
The answer in thirty seconds

A bug class seen and shelved in 2024 was turned into working exploits by three AI-assisted teams within three weeks in August 2026. The disclosure leaked 22.5 hours early. Agencies split on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

Read the site as Blake →

What this incident says about coordinated disclosure once models can find bugs, and once a leak can become a proof of concept faster than a patch can ship. The claims below are the evidence; the reading is the site's.

## What to decide or do
- The window between leak and release was 22.5 hours and the window between first honeypot hit and release was four days. Both are shorter than the two months the fix took.
- Three AI-assisted teams converged on a bug class seen and shelved in 2024. The constraint that failed in 2024 was proving exploitability, and that is what models now appear to lower the cost of.
- The defensive side moved early too: WAF rules 9 hours ahead, images 6 hours ahead (against the embargo), agencies within the hour. The system is faster in both directions.
- The public numbers were not produced for decision-making and should not be used for it; the one agency that counted got about 6,000 in a country of 1.9 million people.
- Agencies diverged on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

# How did coordinated disclosure fail, and what does AI-assisted discovery change?

B
The answer in thirty seconds

A bug class seen and shelved in 2024 was turned into working exploits by three AI-assisted teams within three weeks in August 2026. The disclosure leaked 22.5 hours early. Agencies split on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

Read the site as Blake →

What this incident says about coordinated disclosure once models can find bugs, and once a leak can become a proof of concept faster than a patch can ship. The claims below are the evidence; the reading is the site's.

## What to decide or do
- The window between leak and release was 22.5 hours and the window between first honeypot hit and release was four days. Both are shorter than the two months the fix took.
- Three AI-assisted teams converged on a bug class seen and shelved in 2024. The constraint that failed in 2024 was proving exploitability, and that is what models now appear to lower the cost of.
- The defensive side moved early too: WAF rules 9 hours ahead, images 6 hours ahead (against the embargo), agencies within the hour. The system is faster in both directions.
- The public numbers were not produced for decision-making and should not be used for it; the one agency that counted got about 6,000 in a country of 1.9 million people.
- Agencies diverged on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# How did coordinated disclosure fail, and what does AI-assisted discovery change?

B
The answer in thirty seconds

A bug class seen and shelved in 2024 was turned into working exploits by three AI-assisted teams within three weeks in August 2026. The disclosure leaked 22.5 hours early. Agencies split on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

Read the site as Blake →

What this incident says about coordinated disclosure once models can find bugs, and once a leak can become a proof of concept faster than a patch can ship. The claims below are the evidence; the reading is the site's.

## What to decide or do
- The window between leak and release was 22.5 hours and the window between first honeypot hit and release was four days. Both are shorter than the two months the fix took.
- Three AI-assisted teams converged on a bug class seen and shelved in 2024. The constraint that failed in 2024 was proving exploitability, and that is what models now appear to lower the cost of.
- The defensive side moved early too: WAF rules 9 hours ahead, images 6 hours ahead (against the embargo), agencies within the hour. The system is faster in both directions.
- The public numbers were not produced for decision-making and should not be used for it; the one agency that counted got about 6,000 in a country of 1.9 million people.
- Agencies diverged on the hardest question, offline or not, along lines that look institutional rather than technical.

Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, or, in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities listing of 26 October, of exploitation with no victim named; the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. # The code: where php2shell lives and what the fix does

Read from a clone of php/php-src: the fix commit (389 files, authored 18 October, public 21 October 14:06 UTC), the engine mechanism it replaces, the hunks that matter, and the end-of-life backport.

# The code: where the bug is, and what the fix does

The editor's question was where the flaw actually lives: in PHP, in C, in the engine? The answer, read from the repository rather than from any article, is the Zend engine's memory manager and request lifecycle, in C, below every PHP application. This page is built from a clone of php/php-src: the fix commit, its parent, the branch it landed on, the end-of-life backport, and the diff between the last vulnerable and first fixed release. The patches and the commit metadata are in the vault with their hashes. php/php-src , read from a clone PHP PHP php.net php-src php.net Daubois Fastly Imperva Threat Research OpenAI / Wiz / Calif joint microsi OpenAI on X

## Where the bug is
- **The language a site is written in (PHP code)** ✗ not where the bug is: Not where the bug is. A site's own PHP code can be perfect; php2shell.com's phrase is that a 'Hello World' application on an affected version is affected.
- **The Zend engine (C): memory manager, request start-up and shutdown** ✓ in scope: Where both bugs are. ## What the fix does, step by step

The site's reading of the diff, checked against the two GitHub advisories. Each step names the function or file it comes from; the hunks below are verbatim.
- **Before the fix.** When a request pushed PHP past memory_limit, the allocator called zend_mm_safe_error, which raised a fatal error inside a zend_try and then called zend_bailout(): a C longjmp back to the request's top-level handler. The jump abandons whatever function was half-way through building request state. On mod_php the request shutdown then runs anyway and reads that half-built state. That is CVE-2026-109618, 'RCE via OOM corruption'. The same longjmp, or any fatal error, could leave global state pointing into request memory that is about to be freed; the next request on the same worker reads it. That is CVE-2026-109619, 'RCE via stale global state'.
- **The attacker's lever.** The attacker needs to make the allocator fail at a moment of their choosing. The confirmed ways are request-shaped: a multipart body with many parts or long headers (rfc1867.c), deeply nested form field names (php_variables.c and the hash table), and the session upload-progress feature, which is on by default and does work inside the multipart parser before the application runs. Several vendors say the exploit also needs to know the running binary's layout on x86_64, which is why the CVSS vector says attack complexity high.
- **After the fix: the soft limit.** zend_mm_check_limit no longer jumps. If an allocation would exceed memory_limit (now the soft limit), it queues a 'delayed OOM' error and lets the allocation succeed. At the next VM safe point zend_handle_delayed_oom runs, throws an UnwindExit that unwinds the PHP frames in an orderly way, and raises the fatal error with the request's state intact. The commit's own comment: 'When the soft limit is to be exceeded, a delayed OOM error is queued. When the hard limit is to be exceeded, the function does not return.'
- **After the fix: the hard limit.** A new memory_hard_limit_percent setting defines a ceiling above memory_limit. Reaching it calls zend_mm_hard_limit_error and the process ends with _exit(), with no cleanup to corrupt. Allocations that callers can tolerate failing become 'fallible' and return NULL instead of jumping. zend_mm_panic now also uses _exit rather than exit.
- **After the fix: the globals.** shutdown_executor, php_request_shutdown and sapi_deactivate set the pointers they free to NULL or UNDEF ('may be accessed before php_request_startup()'), so a later request cannot find stale state. A new max_multipart_body_parts setting bounds the number of parts the parser will accept; the multipart header parser keeps only Content-Disposition and Content-Type and ignores duplicates; the session upload-progress callback is changed.

## The end-of-life backport, and how it differs

Branch `PHP-7.4-CVE-2026-109618-109619`, commit `712e60f9e`, same title, same author, authored 2026-10-18 18:09:54 UTC. The commit says *Minimal mitigation for EOL version.*. 17 files: `Zend/zend_alloc.c (+68)`, `Zend/zend_execute_API.c (+13)`, `Zend/zend_hash.c (+13)`, `Zend/zend_types.h (26)`, `Zend/zend_vm_def.h (+11)`, `main/rfc1867.c (+39)`, `main/php_variables.c (8)`, `main/main.c (+6)`, `main/SAPI.c (+5)`, `ext/session/session.c (2)`, `Zend/zend_API.h, zend_alloc.h, zend_hash.h, zend_llist.c, zend_multiply.h, zend_strtod.c, zend_vm_execute.h`. Instead of the delayed error and the unwind, every memory error calls a new `zend_mm_safe_error_ex` that prints the fatal and `_exit`s the process; the same globals are reset; a `max_multipart_body_parts` cap is added; the multipart header parser keeps only the two headers it uses; and the session upload-progress callback is disabled with a one-line `|| true`. A worker that dies on every out-of-memory cannot be exploited this way and will be worse at staying up.

## What the two ledgers say together

- **Precaution was the dominant response**, and it was institutional: national CERTs, state IT providers and councils pulled sites on advice, often before the patch existed, and said so. The one operator who measured it served 94% of its traffic from cache for 13 hours.

- **Attempts are not compromises.** Cloudflare's millions and Amazon's honeypot hits are requests matching a shape at the edge or against a sensor. Nobody has published a count of successful exploitations, and the parties best placed to see one (CISA, Huntress, Imperva) report none.

- **Absence of evidence is weak here.** The detection authors are explicit that default web logs cannot show the attack shape and that no standard log carries the worker id the cross-request bug needs. A quiet log is not a clean host.

- **The question that would settle it** is one that no captured source answers: of the 1.57 million unpatched hosts Censys counted, how many were mod_php on x86_64 with default limits, reachable without a WAF, and how many of those show a worker spawning a shell. That number is what 'blast radius' means at internet scale, and it does not exist yet.

What a compromise of one system would reach is on the blast-radius section; how to tell is on detection and defence.

## What the two ledgers say together

- **Precaution was the dominant response**, and it was institutional: national CERTs, state IT providers and councils pulled sites on advice, often before the patch existed, and said so. The one operator who measured it served 94% of its traffic from cache for 13 hours.

- **Attempts are not compromises.** Cloudflare's millions and Amazon's honeypot hits are requests matching a shape at the edge or against a sensor. Nobody has published a count of successful exploitations, and the parties best placed to see one (CISA, Huntress, Imperva) report none.

- **Absence of evidence is weak here.** The detection authors are explicit that default web logs cannot show the attack shape and that no standard log carries the worker id the cross-request bug needs. A quiet log is not a clean host.

- **The question that would settle it** is one that no captured source answers: of the 1.57 million unpatched hosts Censys counted, how many were mod_php on x86_64 with default limits, reachable without a WAF, and how many of those show a worker spawning a shell. What a compromise of one system would reach is on the blast-radius section; how to tell is on detection and defence.

- **Precaution was the dominant response**, and it was institutional: national CERTs, state IT providers and councils pulled sites on advice, often before the patch existed, and said so. The one operator who measured it served 94% of its traffic from cache for 13 hours.

- **Attempts are not compromises.** Cloudflare's millions and Amazon's honeypot hits are requests matching a shape at the edge or against a sensor. Nobody has published a count of successful exploitations, and the parties best placed to see one (CISA, Huntress, Imperva) report none.

## What the two ledgers say together

- **Precaution was the dominant response**, and it was institutional: national CERTs, state IT providers and councils pulled sites on advice, often before the patch existed, and said so. The one operator who measured it served 94% of its traffic from cache for 13 hours.

- **Attempts are not compromises.** Cloudflare's millions and Amazon's honeypot hits are requests matching a shape at the edge or against a sensor. Nobody has published a count of successful exploitations, and the parties best placed to see one (CISA, Huntress, Imperva) report none.

- **Absence of evidence is weak here.** The detection authors are explicit that default web logs cannot show the attack shape and that no standard log carries the worker id the cross-request bug needs. A quiet log is not a clean host.

- **The question that would settle it** is one that no captured source answers: of the 1.57 million unpatched hosts Censys counted, how many were mod_php on x86_64 with default limits, reachable without a WAF, and how many of those show a worker spawning a shell. That number is what 'blast radius' means at internet scale, and it does not exist yet.

What a compromise of one system would reach is on the blast-radius section; how to tell is on detection and defence.

# Detection and defence: can it be blocked, can it be seen

The editor's premise is that a zero-day is not an invisibility cloak: an exploit that runs code on a web server leaves a request in the log, a crash in the kernel, a child process in the tree. The captured sources agree, and they also say where the logs go blind. This page is what six edge vendors, three community rule sets and one detection guide say about blocking the request, and what the host shows once the request got through.

Every one of them says the same two things: it is a stopgap, and patch anyway. The flaw fires during request set-up, so any URL that reaches PHP is a candidate and a rule can only match shape; a rule that blocks every multipart body also blocks every upload. ## Signatures
- **Community Suricata and Snort rules** (darkfibr/php2shell-detect, rjmendez/phpup-2026, Lexsah/php2shell-detection). Three independent repositories, all keying on request shape rather than payload bytes: the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field plus many array-form parts; duplicate or excessive multipart headers; a PHP worker spawning a shell. rjmendez retired its own earlier rules after finding the leaked proof-of-concept's mechanism did not match the fix. No rule from the Emerging Threats or Snort projects themselves was found. darkfibr , GitHub rjmendez, GitHub Lexsah, GitHub
- **ModSecurity, Sigma, Falco, YARA, auditd** (Blevene's detection guide; Lexsah). A ModSecurity rule on the upload-progress field name (verified on 2.9.14, 'zero false positives by construction' once the feature is off), Sigma rules for the arm-phase fatal error ('in Unknown on line 0' means the bailout happened outside any script, in the multipart parse) and for FPM segfaults, Falco rules for a PHP worker exec or memfd, auditd for execve by the pool user. The guide notes ModSecurity's REQUEST_BODY is empty for multipart requests, so an earlier tripwire that matched it never fired. Blevene Lexsah, GitHub
- **The Hacker News, on what protects before the patch** (The Hacker News). Captured for the record; the newsroom's reading of it is on the exploitation page. THN

## On the host: what exploitation looks like

| Where | Signal | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Access log** | Multipart POSTs to endpoints that do not take uploads; bodies larger than memory_limit ending in 500 or 502; a burst of 500s from one IP followed by a slow 200 | Blevene Fastly |
| **PHP error log** | 'Allowed memory size exhausted ... in Unknown on line 0' (an OOM outside any script, during request parsing); 'Failed to decode session object' | Blevene |
| **Web server and kernel** | Clusters of Apache 'exit signal Segmentation fault (11)' or php-fpm segfaults in dmesg within minutes; nginx 'upstream prematurely closed connection' correlated with a prior fatal from the same IP | Fastly Blevene |
| **Process tree** | A mod_php or php-fpm worker spawning /bin/sh, curl, wget, or executing from memfd; with the known exploits no application code runs, so a shell from a worker is the exploit | CISA Fastly Blevene |
| **Network** | New outbound connections from php-fpm or httpd workers to non-database endpoints | Blevene Imperva Threat Research |
| **What the log cannot show** | nginx's default log format records neither Content-Type nor bodies, so shape-based attempts are invisible there; no standard log carries the worker id the cross-request bug needs; a clean log proves little | darkfibr , GitHub rjmendez, GitHub JPCERT/CC |

## How hard it is to exploit

The sources that temper the headline, and the one that says expect more.
- **The CVE vector.** Attack complexity high (AC:H) and attack requirements present (AT:P): the attacker must defeat a built-in protection and needs conditions beyond the request. CVE record
- **Fastly.** 'the existing PoCs require knowledge of the specific, running PHP binary and address space layout on the server for an attack to yield code execution on x86_64, so most deployments may be safe from RCE. Do not assume this holds true for you. If you operate a 32-bit PHP application, you should likely assume compromise.' Fastly
- **Imperva.** 'Triggering the bug is much easier than turning it into code execution.' A later request must reach the same worker and place carefully shaped data. Five demonstrated techniques, three via upload progress; a memory disclosure of about 67 KB. Imperva Threat Research
- **rjmendez (detection author).** A lab reproduction of the leaked proof-of-concept's precondition produced a clean 200; 'VulnCheck independently reports that none of the public PoCs they reviewed have the correct mechanism'. rjmendez, GitHub
- **Huntress.** Had not built or reproduced a proof of concept and was not aware of public exploit code as of 20:30 UTC on 21 October. Huntress
- **Fastly, on the fix.** 'The PHP source tree calls the zend_bailout mechanism many places'; patching the demonstrated paths 'does not make the mechanism safe'. Expect more paths. Fastly

## So: can it be detected?

Yes, at two layers, and no at a third. **At the edge**, the known request shapes are distinctive and the vendors say their rules match them; the limit is variants and traffic that bypasses the edge. **On the host**, the strongest signal is the one that needs no signature: a PHP worker spawning a shell or a downloader when no application code ran. That is a process-tree rule, cheap to deploy, and the one the detection authors and CISA converge on. **In the default web log**, no: nginx's standard format records neither the content type nor the body, and the cross-request bug leaves no worker id anywhere a log would carry it. An organisation whose only telemetry is the access log cannot answer "were we hit" from it, which is the fact behind the agencies' advice to assess for backdoors rather than to look for a log line.

## On the host: what exploitation looks like

| Where | Signal | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Access log** | Multipart POSTs to endpoints that do not take uploads; bodies larger than memory_limit ending in 500 or 502; a burst of 500s from one IP followed by a slow 200 | Blevene Fastly |
| **PHP error log** | 'Allowed memory size exhausted ... in Unknown on line 0' (an OOM outside any script, during request parsing); 'Failed to decode session object' | Blevene |
| **Web server and kernel** | Clusters of Apache 'exit signal Segmentation fault (11)' or php-fpm segfaults in dmesg within minutes; nginx 'upstream prematurely closed connection' correlated with a prior fatal from the same IP | Fastly Blevene |

## How hard it is to exploit

The sources that temper the headline, and the one that says expect more.
- **The CVE vector.** Attack complexity high (AC:H) and attack requirements present (AT:P): the attacker must defeat a built-in protection and needs conditions beyond the request. CVE record
- **Fastly.** 'the existing PoCs require knowledge of the specific, running PHP binary and address space layout on the server for an attack to yield code execution on x86_64, so most deployments may be safe from RCE. - **Imperva.** 'Triggering the bug is much easier than turning it into code execution.' A later request must reach the same worker and place carefully shaped data. Five demonstrated techniques, three via upload progress; a memory disclosure of about 67 KB. Imperva Threat Research

- **Huntress.** Had not built or reproduced a proof of concept and was not aware of public exploit code as of 20:30 UTC on 21 October. Huntress

## What the comparison says

The site's reading of the table above. Positions, with the evidence attached.
- Severity is not exposure. php2shell's 9.2 is a property of the bug; Heartbleed's 'everyone' and Log4Shell's 'everywhere' were properties of deployment. The comparators show both kinds of big: a bug in a runtime that everything sits on (Log4Shell, Shellshock, php2shell) and a bug whose real exposure was a narrow configuration (CVE-2019-11043, Spring4Shell, CVE-2024-4577 on Windows CGI). Which kind php2shell is depends on how many of the 1.57 million unpatched hosts Censys counted are mod_php on x86_64 with the default settings, a number nobody has published.
- Urgency before disclosure was institutional, not public. The PHP project had the fix on 18 October and sat on it for a coordinated release; Cloudflare had rules live nine hours early; Amazon had honeypot hits four days early; agencies published within the hour. That is the Kaminsky model working as designed, right up to the point it leaked. The public alarm came with the agencies' offline advice on the morning of 22 October, which is why the editor's question, 'why was the alarm only raised when it went public', has a factual answer: because the embargo held for everyone who was inside it.
- The KEV test. CISA lists a CVE when it has reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. Log4Shell and MOVEit were listed the day they were published; CVE-2024-4577 in three days. php2shell was not listed after one day, with Amazon saying it is 'broadly exploited' against honeypots and NCSC NZ 'aware of reports'. Either the evidence has not reached CISA's bar, or attempts against sensors are not the same as exploitation of victims. This site will record the day it is added, if it is.
- What is new is not the bug class but the discovery pipeline. The OOM-bailout pattern was seen in 2024 and shelved because nobody could prove exploitation. Three teams with model assistance proved it inside three weeks of each other. The historical comparison that matters is therefore not Heartbleed but the gap between 'theoretically exploitable' and 'proven', which used to be months of expert work and may now be days.

The signals that would move php2shell into the catalog are on the exploitation page; what was taken offline, and by whom, is on impact.

## What the comparison says

The site's reading of the table above. Positions, with the evidence attached.
- Severity is not exposure. php2shell's 9.2 is a property of the bug; Heartbleed's 'everyone' and Log4Shell's 'everywhere' were properties of deployment. Which kind php2shell is depends on how many of the 1.57 million unpatched hosts Censys counted are mod_php on x86_64 with the default settings, a number nobody has published.
- Urgency before disclosure was institutional, not public. The PHP project had the fix on 18 October and sat on it for a coordinated release; Cloudflare had rules live nine hours early; Amazon had honeypot hits four days early; agencies published within the hour. That is the Kaminsky model working as designed, right up to the point it leaked. The public alarm came with the agencies' offline advice on the morning of 22 October, which is why the editor's question, 'why was the alarm only raised when it went public', has a factual answer: because the embargo held for everyone who was inside it.
- The KEV test. CISA lists a CVE when it has reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. Log4Shell and MOVEit were listed the day they were published; CVE-2024-4577 in three days. php2shell was not listed after one day, with Amazon saying it is 'broadly exploited' against honeypots and NCSC NZ 'aware of reports'. Either the evidence has not reached CISA's bar, or attempts against sensors are not the same as exploitation of victims. This site will record the day it is added, if it is.
- What is new is not the bug class but the discovery pipeline. The OOM-bailout pattern was seen in 2024 and shelved because nobody could prove exploitation. Three teams with model assistance proved it inside three weeks of each other. The historical comparison that matters is therefore not Heartbleed but the gap between 'theoretically exploitable' and 'proven', which used to be months of expert work and may now be days.

The signals that would move php2shell into the catalog are on the exploitation page; what was taken offline, and by whom, is on impact.

## What the comparison says

The site's reading of the table above. Positions, with the evidence attached.
- Severity is not exposure. php2shell's 9.2 is a property of the bug; Heartbleed's 'everyone' and Log4Shell's 'everywhere' were properties of deployment. The comparators show both kinds of big: a bug in a runtime that everything sits on (Log4Shell, Shellshock, php2shell) and a bug whose real exposure was a narrow configuration (CVE-2019-11043, Spring4Shell, CVE-2024-4577 on Windows CGI). Which kind php2shell is depends on how many of the 1.57 million unpatched hosts Censys counted are mod_php on x86_64 with the default settings, a number nobody has published.
- Urgency before disclosure was institutional, not public. The PHP project had the fix on 18 October and sat on it for a coordinated release; Cloudflare had rules live nine hours early; Amazon had honeypot hits four days early; agencies published within the hour. That is the Kaminsky model working as designed, right up to the point it leaked. The public alarm came with the agencies' offline advice on the morning of 22 October, which is why the editor's question, 'why was the alarm only raised when it went public', has a factual answer: because the embargo held for everyone who was inside it.
- The KEV test. CISA lists a CVE when it has reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. Log4Shell and MOVEit were listed the day they were published; CVE-2024-4577 in three days. php2shell was not listed after one day, with Amazon saying it is 'broadly exploited' against honeypots and NCSC NZ 'aware of reports'. Either the evidence has not reached CISA's bar, or attempts against sensors are not the same as exploitation of victims. This site will record the day it is added, if it is.
- What is new is not the bug class but the discovery pipeline. The OOM-bailout pattern was seen in 2024 and shelved because nobody could prove exploitation. Three teams with model assistance proved it inside three weeks of each other. The historical comparison that matters is therefore not Heartbleed but the gap between 'theoretically exploitable' and 'proven', which used to be months of expert work and may now be days.

The signals that would move php2shell into the catalog are on the exploitation page; what was taken offline, and by whom, is on impact.

# Briefing for a ciso: What is our exposure, what is our evidence we were not hit, and what do I tell the board?

The php2shell story for a ciso: what to decide, the claims it rests on with their status and sources, and what is still open.

Briefing · CISO

# What is our exposure, what is our evidence we were not hit, and what do I tell the board?

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## The facts this rests on
- confirmed two or more primary sources agree, or the fact was counted from a captured file
- reported one party says so, and it has not been contradicted
- disputed the sources disagree, and both readings are shown
- contradicted a primary source says otherwise
- unverified even the reporting outlet could not check it
- p/n primary sources among the n cited; a blocked capture is counted and marked

R
The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post. No copy of that post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The BBC's list (parts of Wikipedia, Edinburgh council, French government services, the University of Geneva, the BBC itself) has not been captured from any of those organisations. Latvia's geo-blocking is the one documented case, from the agency itself.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

R
The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post. No copy of that post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The BBC's list (parts of Wikipedia, Edinburgh council, French government services, the University of Geneva, the BBC itself) has not been captured from any of those organisations. Latvia's geo-blocking is the one documented case, from the agency itself.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

# What is our exposure, what is our evidence we were not hit, and what do I tell the board?

R
The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). # What is our exposure, what is our evidence we were not hit, and what do I tell the board?

R
The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The answer in thirty seconds

The flaw is in the PHP runtime, so exposure is every internet-facing system running PHP, including vendor appliances. Review logs from 17 October (the earliest reported attempt), not from the fix. Attempts are reported at scale; no named victim is confirmed. Patch first, isolate where you cannot.

Read the site as Robin →

Exposure, evidence of non-compromise, and the board message. Three facts carry this briefing: the bug is in the runtime so your application code is not the question; attempts are in the millions at one CDN but no named victim is confirmed anywhere; and every agency says patch first, with offline as the fallback not the reflex.

## What to decide or do
- Exposure is a list, not a percentage: every internet-facing system serving PHP, with SAPI, version and what sits behind it. Vendor appliances and hosting panels count.
- Evidence of non-compromise means log review from 17 October (Amazon's earliest attempt), not from the 21st, and host checks for shells spawned by PHP workers, not just WAF hits.
- The board line: a critical runtime flaw, patched on day one where we could, isolated where we could not, no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing. Do not quote 70%.
- Edge rules were live hours before disclosure; if you are behind a major CDN you had a stopgap you did not have to ask for. It is not a control you can rely on.
- Expect a follow-up release: a report that the first fix is incomplete reached the security list within two hours.

- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, or, in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities listing of 26 October, of exploitation with no victim named; the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# What does this cost us in engineering time, what breaks when we patch, and what do we change so the next one is a non-event?

What the patch changes, what it breaks, and what to change afterwards. The fix is a redesign of how PHP handles running out of memory, so behaviour under memory pressure changes, and it touched 389 files.

## What to decide or do
- Patch order: mod_php on the internet first; FPM next; everything else after. Restart every worker, rebuild every image, then verify the running version inside the container.
- The new memory_hard_limit_percent and max_multipart_body_parts settings exist now; the defaults are conservative, and a system that used to survive on the edge of memory_limit may now _exit instead.
- 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have a source backport and no release: that is a migration you are now doing, not a patch.
- The engineering lesson is time-to-pull-the-plug: how long it takes to take one system off the internet cleanly, with a holding page and a way back, is a property of your platform and it was measured this week whether you wanted it or not.
- What to change: an inventory that answers "where is PHP" in minutes; worker-process monitoring (a PHP worker spawning a shell is the signal); a rehearsed isolate runbook with a named owner.
