# What does this cost us in engineering time, what breaks when we patch, and what do we change so the next one is a non-event?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Patch internet-facing mod_php first, then FPM, then the rest; restart every worker and rebuild every image. The fix changes how PHP behaves when memory runs out, so test under load. 7.4 to 8.1 have no release. Afterwards, invest in an inventory that answers 'where is PHP' in minutes.

Read the site as Avery →

What the patch changes, what it breaks, and what to change afterwards. The fix is a redesign of how PHP handles running out of memory, so behaviour under memory pressure changes, and it touched 389 files.

## What to decide or do
- Patch order: mod_php on the internet first; FPM next; everything else after. Restart every worker, rebuild every image, then verify the running version inside the container.
- The new memory_hard_limit_percent and max_multipart_body_parts settings exist now; the defaults are conservative, and a system that used to survive on the edge of memory_limit may now _exit instead.
- 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have a source backport and no release: that is a migration you are now doing, not a patch.
- The engineering lesson is time-to-pull-the-plug: how long it takes to take one system off the internet cleanly, with a holding page and a way back, is a property of your platform and it was measured this week whether you wanted it or not.
- What to change: an inventory that answers "where is PHP" in minutes; worker-process monitoring (a PHP worker spawning a shell is the signal); a rehearsed isolate runbook with a named owner.

# What does this cost us in engineering time, what breaks when we patch, and what do we change so the next one is a non-event?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Patch internet-facing mod_php first, then FPM, then the rest; restart every worker and rebuild every image. The fix changes how PHP behaves when memory runs out, so test under load. 7.4 to 8.1 have no release. Afterwards, invest in an inventory that answers 'where is PHP' in minutes.

Read the site as Avery →

What the patch changes, what it breaks, and what to change afterwards. The fix is a redesign of how PHP handles running out of memory, so behaviour under memory pressure changes, and it touched 389 files.

## What to decide or do
- Patch order: mod_php on the internet first; FPM next; everything else after. Restart every worker, rebuild every image, then verify the running version inside the container.
- The new memory_hard_limit_percent and max_multipart_body_parts settings exist now; the defaults are conservative, and a system that used to survive on the edge of memory_limit may now _exit instead.
- 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have a source backport and no release: that is a migration you are now doing, not a patch.
- The engineering lesson is time-to-pull-the-plug: how long it takes to take one system off the internet cleanly, with a holding page and a way back, is a property of your platform and it was measured this week whether you wanted it or not.
- What to change: an inventory that answers "where is PHP" in minutes; worker-process monitoring (a PHP worker spawning a shell is the signal); a rehearsed isolate runbook with a named owner.

# What does this cost us in engineering time, what breaks when we patch, and what do we change so the next one is a non-event?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Patch internet-facing mod_php first, then FPM, then the rest; restart every worker and rebuild every image. The fix changes how PHP behaves when memory runs out, so test under load. 7.4 to 8.1 have no release. Afterwards, invest in an inventory that answers 'where is PHP' in minutes.

Read the site as Avery →

What the patch changes, what it breaks, and what to change afterwards. The fix is a redesign of how PHP handles running out of memory, so behaviour under memory pressure changes, and it touched 389 files.

## What to decide or do
- Patch order: mod_php on the internet first; FPM next; everything else after. Restart every worker, rebuild every image, then verify the running version inside the container.
- The new memory_hard_limit_percent and max_multipart_body_parts settings exist now; the defaults are conservative, and a system that used to survive on the edge of memory_limit may now _exit instead.
- 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have a source backport and no release: that is a migration you are now doing, not a patch.
- The engineering lesson is time-to-pull-the-plug: how long it takes to take one system off the internet cleanly, with a holding page and a way back, is a property of your platform and it was measured this week whether you wanted it or not.
- What to change: an inventory that answers "where is PHP" in minutes; worker-process monitoring (a PHP worker spawning a shell is the signal); a rehearsed isolate runbook with a named owner.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. No named organisation has confirmed a compromise. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of the evening of 22 October, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of the evening of 22 October, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of the evening of 22 October, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# What is the financial exposure, what does downtime cost against breach cost, and will insurance respond?

Q
The answer in thirty seconds

The documented cost so far is precaution, not breach: hours to a day of downtime for organisations that pulled sites, and engineering time to update. As of 14:42 UTC on 26 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through this flaw. Ask your broker now, in writing, whether a precautionary shutdown with no breach is covered. Do not use 70% of the Internet in any forecast.

Read the site as Quinn →

The financial question has two sides and the evidence is lopsided: downtime is documented and measurable; breach is claimed and unconfirmed. Insurers are already treating this as an aggregation event.

## What to decide or do
- Cost of acting: operators that pulled sites report hours to a day offline; one operator served 94% of its page views from cache through a 13-hour shutdown. Engineering time to patch, restart and verify is the main cost for most.
- Cost of not acting: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the web tier; what it reaches is whatever that tier can reach, which is a question for the CISO's inventory, not for a percentage.
- Insurance: Insurance Business reports underwriters watching for an aggregation event and asks whether business-interruption cover responds to a precautionary shutdown with no breach; that depends on wording and waiting periods. Ask the broker now, in writing.
- Figures you will hear and should not use in a forecast: 70% of the Internet (a share of websites restated), 30 million websites (no basis), 22.6 million systems (method not given). Use your own inventory count.
- No named organisation has confirmed a compromise as of the latest capture. That is a statement about evidence, not about safety.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, or, in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities listing of 26 October, of exploitation with no victim named; the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# Briefing for a head of appsec: Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

Briefing · Head of AppSec

# Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

Scope, settings and the pipeline change. The bug is below your applications: any PHP endpoint that reaches the runtime is a candidate, and the demonstrated paths run before application code.

## What to decide or do
- In scope: every application on an affected runtime, including the ones with no uploads and no sessions; the session upload-progress path is on by default and needs no session_start().
- Settings that bound the known paths, in the order of least breakage: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (server-level, not ini_set); post_max_size low; max_input_nesting_level low; max_multipart_body_parts on patched builds; fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5; pm.max_requests on FPM. None is a fix.
- The runtime version in production is now an application-security finding: add it to the SBOM, fail the pipeline on an unfixed PHP, and check the running version after deploy, not the package version before.
- Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app: the request shape (upload-progress field plus many array parts, oversized multipart bodies) and the process tree (a worker spawning a shell).
- The public proof-of-concept code does not work as published, per VulnCheck and a lab reproduction; a scanner that fires on it is testing the wrong thing.

# Briefing for a head of appsec: Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

The php2shell story for a head of appsec: a thirty-second answer, what to decide, a reading path, the claims it rests on with their status and sources, and what is still open.

Briefing for Jamie, head of appsec · ******Deeply technical

# Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

J
The answer in thirty seconds

Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

Read the site as Jamie →

Scope, settings and the pipeline change. The bug is below your applications: any PHP endpoint that reaches the runtime is a candidate, and the demonstrated paths run before application code.

## What to decide or do
- In scope: every application on an affected runtime, including the ones with no uploads and no sessions; the session upload-progress path is on by default and needs no session_start().
- Settings that bound the known paths, in the order of least breakage: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (server-level, not ini_set); post_max_size low; max_input_nesting_level low; max_multipart_body_parts on patched builds; fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5; pm.max_requests on FPM. None is a fix.
- The runtime version in production is now an application-security finding: add it to the SBOM, fail the pipeline on an unfixed PHP, and check the running version after deploy, not the package version before.
- Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app: the request shape (upload-progress field plus many array parts, oversized multipart bodies) and the process tree (a worker spawning a shell).
- The public proof-of-concept code does not work as published, per VulnCheck and a lab reproduction; a scanner that fires on it is testing the wrong thing.

# Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

J
The answer in thirty seconds

Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

Read the site as Jamie →

Scope, settings and the pipeline change. The bug is below your applications: any PHP endpoint that reaches the runtime is a candidate, and the demonstrated paths run before application code.

## What to decide or do
- In scope: every application on an affected runtime, including the ones with no uploads and no sessions; the session upload-progress path is on by default and needs no session_start().
- Settings that bound the known paths, in the order of least breakage: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (server-level, not ini_set); post_max_size low; max_input_nesting_level low; max_multipart_body_parts on patched builds; fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5; pm.max_requests on FPM. None is a fix.
- The runtime version in production is now an application-security finding: add it to the SBOM, fail the pipeline on an unfixed PHP, and check the running version after deploy, not the package version before.
- Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app: the request shape (upload-progress field plus many array parts, oversized multipart bodies) and the process tree (a worker spawning a shell).
- The public proof-of-concept code does not work as published, per VulnCheck and a lab reproduction; a scanner that fires on it is testing the wrong thing.

# Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

J
The answer in thirty seconds

Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

Read the site as Jamie →

Scope, settings and the pipeline change. The bug is below your applications: any PHP endpoint that reaches the runtime is a candidate, and the demonstrated paths run before application code.

## What to decide or do
- In scope: every application on an affected runtime, including the ones with no uploads and no sessions; the session upload-progress path is on by default and needs no session_start().
- Settings that bound the known paths, in the order of least breakage: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (server-level, not ini_set); post_max_size low; max_input_nesting_level low; max_multipart_body_parts on patched builds; fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5; pm.max_requests on FPM. None is a fix.
- The runtime version in production is now an application-security finding: add it to the SBOM, fail the pipeline on an unfixed PHP, and check the running version after deploy, not the package version before.
- Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app: the request shape (upload-progress field plus many array parts, oversized multipart bodies) and the process tree (a worker spawning a shell).
- The public proof-of-concept code does not work as published, per VulnCheck and a lab reproduction; a scanner that fires on it is testing the wrong thing.

# Briefing for a head of AppSec: Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

The php2shell story for a head of AppSec: a thirty-second answer, what to decide, a reading path, the claims it rests on with their status and sources, and what is still open.

Briefing for Jamie, head of appsec · ******Deeply technical

# Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

J
The answer in thirty seconds

Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

Read the site as Jamie →

Scope, settings and the pipeline change. The bug is below your applications: any PHP endpoint that reaches the runtime is a candidate, and the demonstrated paths run before application code.

## What to decide or do
- In scope: every application on an affected runtime, including the ones with no uploads and no sessions; the session upload-progress path is on by default and needs no session_start().
- Settings that bound the known paths, in the order of least breakage: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (server-level, not ini_set); post_max_size low; max_input_nesting_level low; max_multipart_body_parts on patched builds; fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5; pm.max_requests on FPM. None is a fix.
- The runtime version in production is now an application-security finding: add it to the SBOM, fail the pipeline on an unfixed PHP, and check the running version after deploy, not the package version before.
- Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app: the request shape (upload-progress field plus many array parts, oversized multipart bodies) and the process tree (a worker spawning a shell).
- The public proof-of-concept code does not work as published, per VulnCheck and a lab reproduction; a scanner that fires on it is testing the wrong thing.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# Which of our applications are in scope, which settings matter, and what do we add to the pipeline?

J
The answer in thirty seconds

Every application on an affected runtime is in scope, including ones with no uploads or sessions: the demonstrated paths run before application code. Add the running PHP version to the SBOM and fail the pipeline on an unfixed one. Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app.

Read the site as Jamie →

Scope, settings and the pipeline change. The bug is below your applications: any PHP endpoint that reaches the runtime is a candidate, and the demonstrated paths run before application code.

## What to decide or do
- In scope: every application on an affected runtime, including the ones with no uploads and no sessions; the session upload-progress path is on by default and needs no session_start().
- Settings that bound the known paths, in the order of least breakage: session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (server-level, not ini_set); post_max_size low; max_input_nesting_level low; max_multipart_body_parts on patched builds; fatal_error_backtraces=0 on 8.5; pm.max_requests on FPM. None is a fix.
- The runtime version in production is now an application-security finding: add it to the SBOM, fail the pipeline on an unfixed PHP, and check the running version after deploy, not the package version before.
- Detection belongs at the edge and on the host, not in the app: the request shape (upload-progress field plus many array parts, oversized multipart bodies) and the process tree (a worker spawning a shell).
- The public proof-of-concept code does not work as published, per VulnCheck and a lab reproduction; a scanner that fires on it is testing the wrong thing.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, or, in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities listing of 26 October, of exploitation with no victim named; the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# Is my code the problem, what do I change, and how do I check the box I deployed to?

Your code is not the problem and cannot be the fix. The flaw is in the C engine that runs it. What you can do is check the box you deploy to and avoid making the engine's job harder.

## What to decide or do
- Check the running version where the code runs: php -v inside the container or phpinfo() on the box, after the restart. The package list is not the answer.
- Fixed: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. If your target is 8.1 or older there is no release; tell whoever owns the platform today.
- Nothing in userland blocks the demonstrated paths: ini_set() runs too late, .user.ini runs too late, auto_prepend_file runs too late. The settings have to be in php.ini, the pool or the server config.
- Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and timeouts in your own code anyway: the advisory lists them as one of the paths for the stale-state bug.
- After the patch, out-of-memory behaves differently: a delayed fatal at the next safe point instead of an abort, and a hard limit that ends the process. Code that caught the old behaviour in tests will see a change.

# Briefing for a media and communications team: What can we say that is true, what should we not say, and what will we be asked?

The php2shell story for a media and communications team: what to decide, the claims it rests on with their status and sources, and what is still open.

Briefing · Media and communications team

# What can we say that is true, what should we not say, and what will we be asked?

What is true, what is not, and what you will be asked. The story most readers saw on the morning of 22 October carried three things this site could not confirm, and the questions will come from that story.

## What to decide or do
- True and safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP itself, patched on 21 October; the organisation patched or isolated its systems; no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing.
- Not safe to say: "70% of the Internet" (a headline restating a share of websites), "the most severe ever" (a vendor's phrase), "exploited everywhere" (attempts against honeypots and CDNs, no named victim), "found by AI" without "by researchers using".

Safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP were fixed on 21 October; we updated or isolated our systems; we have no evidence of compromise and review continues. Do not say '70% of the Internet', 'the most severe ever' or 'exploited everywhere'. Point people to php.net and your national agency.

What is true, what is not, and what you will be asked. The story most readers saw on the morning of 22 October carried three things this site could not confirm, and the questions will come from that story.

## What to decide or do
- True and safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP itself, patched on 21 October; the organisation patched or isolated its systems; no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing.
- Not safe to say: "70% of the Internet" (a headline restating a share of websites), "the most severe ever" (a vendor's phrase), "exploited everywhere" (attempts against honeypots and CDNs, no named victim), "found by AI" without "by researchers using".
- The questions: Were you hit? (answer with the evidence window: logs reviewed from 17 October.) Did you take sites down? (precaution, not incident, as Oxford City Council put it.) Why did it take so long? (the fix was authored on 18 October and released under a coordinated plan that leaked.)
- Attribution: three research teams and the PHP Foundation each tell the discovery story differently; do not pick one. The flaw was seen in 2024 and not fixed because exploitation could not be shown.
- Point at primary sources: php.net's advisory and your national agency. Do not link a vendor blog as the authority.

## What is still open

- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). R
The answer in thirty seconds

Safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP were fixed on 21 October; we updated or isolated our systems; we have no evidence of compromise and review continues. Do not say '70% of the Internet', 'the most severe ever' or 'exploited everywhere'. Point people to php.net and your national agency.

Read the site as Riley →

What is true, what is not, and what you will be asked. The story most readers saw on the morning of 22 October carried three things this site could not confirm, and the questions will come from that story.

## What to decide or do
- True and safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP itself, patched on 21 October; the organisation patched or isolated its systems; no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing.
- Not safe to say: "70% of the Internet" (a headline restating a share of websites), "the most severe ever" (a vendor's phrase), "exploited everywhere" (attempts against honeypots and CDNs, no named victim), "found by AI" without "by researchers using".
- The questions: Were you hit? (answer with the evidence window: logs reviewed from 17 October.) Did you take sites down? (precaution, not incident, as Oxford City Council put it.) Why did it take so long? (the fix was authored on 18 October and released under a coordinated plan that leaked.)
- Attribution: three research teams and the PHP Foundation each tell the discovery story differently; do not pick one. The flaw was seen in 2024 and not fixed because exploitation could not be shown.
- Point at primary sources: php.net's advisory and your national agency. Do not link a vendor blog as the authority.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

What is true, what is not, and what you will be asked. The story most readers saw on the morning of 22 October carried three things this site could not confirm, and the questions will come from that story.

## What to decide or do
- True and safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP itself, patched on 21 October; the organisation patched or isolated its systems; no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing.
- Not safe to say: "70% of the Internet" (a headline restating a share of websites), "the most severe ever" (a vendor's phrase), "exploited everywhere" (attempts against honeypots and CDNs, no named victim), "found by AI" without "by researchers using".
- The questions: Were you hit? (answer with the evidence window: logs reviewed from 17 October.) Did you take sites down? (precaution, not incident, as Oxford City Council put it.) Why did it take so long? (the fix was authored on 18 October and released under a coordinated plan that leaked.)
- Attribution: three research teams and the PHP Foundation each tell the discovery story differently; do not pick one. The flaw was seen in 2024 and not fixed because exploitation could not be shown.
- Point at primary sources: php.net's advisory and your national agency. Do not link a vendor blog as the authority.

- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. Nothing from PHP on the list yet.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

What is true, what is not, and what you will be asked. The story most readers saw on the morning of 22 October carried three things this site could not confirm, and the questions will come from that story.

## What to decide or do
- True and safe to say: two critical flaws in PHP itself, patched on 21 October; the organisation patched or isolated its systems; no evidence of compromise as of today, review continuing.
- Not safe to say: "70% of the Internet" (a headline restating a share of websites), "the most severe ever" (a vendor's phrase), "exploited everywhere" (attempts against honeypots and CDNs, no named victim), "found by AI" without "by researchers using".
- The questions: Were you hit? (answer with the evidence window: logs reviewed from 17 October.) Did you take sites down? (precaution, not incident, as Oxford City Council put it.) Why did it take so long? (the fix was authored on 18 October and released under a coordinated plan that leaked.)
- Attribution: three research teams and the PHP Foundation each tell the discovery story differently; do not pick one. The flaw was seen in 2024 and not fixed because exploitation could not be shown.
- Point at primary sources: php.net's advisory and your national agency. Do not link a vendor blog as the authority.

Every sentence above rests on these rows. They are folded away because they are written in the sources' own vocabulary; the glossary explains each term.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, or, in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities listing of 26 October, of exploitation with no victim named; the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. # php2shell, explained from scratch

No technical background assumed: what PHP is, what went wrong, why it is called php2shell, what the CVE numbers mean, why websites went offline, whether anyone was hacked, and what to do now.

Start here · ******Plain English

# php2shell, explained from scratch

No technical background assumed. Seven short answers, in the order people usually ask them, each linking to the page with the evidence. Words in the dotted underline are explained when you hover or tap them.

What is PHP?What went wrong?Why php2shell?What are the numbers?Why did sites go offline?Was anyone hacked?What happens now?How to read this site

## 1. What is PHP, and is it on my computer?

PHP is a programming language for websites. When you open a page on a site built with it, a program on the website's server, written in PHP, puts the page together (your name, the latest posts, the basket) and sends the result to your browser. WordPress, which runs a very large number of blogs, shops and company sites, is written in PHP; so are Drupal, Joomla, Moodle, Magento and the software behind Wikipedia.

**PHP runs on servers, not on your phone or laptop.** This story is about the organisations that run websites. Visitors are affected only indirectly: if a site they use is broken into, or is taken offline as a precaution.

A normal visitYour browserasks for a page→The website's server, running PHPbuilds the page→Database and filesthe site's content and settings

## 2. What went wrong?

Two bugs were found deep inside PHP itself, not in any one website. Both are in how PHP cleans up after something goes wrong while it is handling a request.

An analogy. Think of PHP as the kitchen behind every page a website serves. When an order is impossible (it needs more than the kitchen is allowed to use), the cook abandons it. The flaws are in how the kitchen abandons and tidies up: in some cases it leaves the counter half cleared, and the next step, or the next order, uses what was left as if it were fresh. A customer who knows this can send an order designed to leave exactly the right things on the counter, so that the kitchen ends up following the customer's instructions instead of the menu.

The attackAnyone on the internetno account, no password→A crafted requestpushes PHP into its error path→The clean-up goes wrongleftover memory is trusted→The attacker's commands runon the server, as the website
What that can reach- the website's own code and settings
- passwords stored in those settings, such as the database's
- files the website can read or write
- other systems that trust this server
What it does not automatically reach- systems the server is not allowed to talk to
- passwords that were never on that server
- your own phone or computer

In the jargon, this is *unauthenticated remote code execution*: no login needed, from anywhere, and the attacker's code runs. It is the most serious kind of flaw there is, which is why the response was so loud. The researchers proved it end to end against the most traditional way of running PHP, inside the Apache web server, before any of the website's own code had run. That last point matters: **it does not matter how well a website is written**; if PHP underneath it is unpatched, it is in scope. php.net PHP PHP

The technical version is on the two flaws, and the code itself on the code.

## 3. Why is it called php2shell?

Serious flaws get nicknames so people can talk about them: Heartbleed, Shellshock, Log4Shell. **php2shell** reads as *PHP to shell*. A shell is the command line an administrator types into; getting a shell on a server means being able to run commands on it. So the name is the whole attack in one word: start with a PHP website, end with a command line on its server. The US NSA wrote it PHP2Shell. NSA Cyber on X Calif

## 4. What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

They are the official names. A CVE number is a serial number for a security flaw, so that vendors, governments and journalists know they mean the same bug: CVE, the year the number was reserved, and a sequence number. Each has a public record saying what is affected and how bad it is.

### CVE-2026-109618

PHP running out of memory mid-request can leave memory half set up, and the clean-up that follows can be steered by an attacker. Severity 9.2 out of 10.

### CVE-2026-109619

Leftover settings from one visitor's request can point at memory that has been released, and the next request on the same worker uses it. Severity 9.2 out of 10.

Both are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, released on 21 October 2026. Older versions (8.1 and before) are past their support date and got no ready-made fix. CVE record CVE record php.net

## 5. Why did governments tell people to take websites offline?

Because an unpatched website with this flaw can be taken over by anyone, and updating every server takes time. The US NSA and CISA said: if you cannot update, take the system offline until you can. The UK's NCSC put that fourth on its list, after updating and temporary fixes; several European agencies said isolate it; others did not mention it at all. Dutch government services, including the DigiD login many Dutch citizens use, were taken offline as a precaution. NSA Cyber on X CISA NCSC UK Rijksoverheid / NCSC-NL

Taking a site offline is a decision an organisation makes, not evidence it was attacked. The agencies page sets the sixteen sets of advice side by side.

## 6. Was anyone actually hacked?

Not that anyone has confirmed, as of the latest evidence this site holds. Attackers have certainly been trying: Cloudflare says it saw millions of attempts across its network, and Amazon says a decoy server was hit four days before the fix was public. But an attempt is not a success, no named organisation has said it was broken into, and the US list of flaws known to be exploited did not include either of these when last checked. That can change quickly, and this site will say so when the evidence does. Matthew Prince , Cloudflare CEO on THN CISA

The details: who went offline and who was compromised, and every sign of exploitation, in order.

## 7. What happens now?

- **If you only use websites:** nothing to do. Ignore messages that tell you to install anything because of this; that is a scam pattern.

- **If you own a website:** ask whoever hosts it whether PHP has been updated and restarted. The website owner's briefing has the exact question to send.

- **If you run systems:** update, restart, verify, and look for signs of compromise. The step-by-step list has every agency's advice in order.

- **If you decide or communicate:** pick your briefing.

## How to read this site

Every statement on this site carries one of five words, so you can tell a fact from a rumour at a glance:

- confirmed two or more primary sources agree, or the fact was counted from a captured file
- reported one party says so, and it has not been contradicted
- disputed the sources disagree, and both readings are shown
- contradicted a primary source says otherwise
- unverified even the reporting outlet could not check it
- p/n primary sources among the n cited; a blocked capture is counted and marked

Every one of those statements links to the pages it comes from, and every one of those pages was saved, dated and fingerprinted when it was read, so that it can be checked later even if the original changes. How that works.

versions.text:
# Glossary: every php2shell term in plain English

40 terms from the php2shell story (PHP, CVE, CVSS, remote code execution, WAF, KEV and more), each explained in plain English, in the sense it has in this story.

Start here · ******Plain English

# Glossary: every term, in plain English

40 words this story cannot avoid, each explained for someone who has never worked in security, and each in the sense it has in this story. On every other page, the first use of each of these words is underlined and links here.

BCEGHKLMNOPRSUVWZ

## B

### Backport

A fix copied to an older version. PHP published source-only backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, with no official release.

When software is out of support, its maintainers usually stop fixing it. For php2shell the PHP project published the fix as source code for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 but no ready-to-install release, so anyone on those versions has to build it themselves or rely on a Linux distribution that does.

Where it matters in this story →

## C

### CDN

Content delivery network: a service such as Cloudflare or Akamai that sits in front of many websites, caching pages and filtering traffic.

A CDN keeps copies of a website's pages close to its visitors and screens the traffic on the way in. Because so much of the web sits behind a few CDNs, their firewall rules protected many sites before their owners did anything.

Where it matters in this story →

### CERT

Computer Emergency Response Team: a national or sector body that coordinates the response to cyber incidents.

CERT-EU, CERT-FR, CERT.LV and JPCERT/CC are examples. They publish alerts, collect reports of attacks and advise organisations in their country or sector.

Where it matters in this story →

### CISA

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

CISA is the US federal agency responsible for civilian cyber defence. It told organisations to take PHP systems offline if they could not patch, and keeps the KEV catalog.

Where it matters in this story → · the authority ↗

### Confirmed, reported, disputed, unverified

The five words this site uses for how far a claim can be trusted.

Confirmed: two or more primary sources agree, or the site counted it from a captured file. Reported: one party says so and nobody has contradicted it. Disputed: sources disagree, and both readings are shown. Contradicted: a primary source says otherwise. Unverified: even the outlet reporting it could not check it.

Where it matters in this story →

### Coordinated disclosure

Keeping a flaw secret between the finders and the maintainers until a fix is ready, then publishing both at an agreed time.

The agreed time is the embargo. For php2shell it was set for 22 October at 14:00 UTC. The CVE numbers leaked on 20 October, so the release was moved forward a day. The leak page reconstructs how.

Where it matters in this story →

### CVE

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public catalogue that gives each known security flaw a unique ID, such as CVE-2026-109618.

A CVE ID is a serial number for a security flaw, so that a vendor, a government agency and a journalist can be sure they are talking about the same bug. The format is CVE, the year the number was reserved, and a sequence number. This story has two: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Each has an official record that says what is affected and how severe it is.

Where it matters in this story → · the authority ↗

### CVSS

Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a severity score from 0 to 10. Both flaws score 9.2, which is rated critical.

CVSS turns the technical details of a flaw (can it be reached over the internet, does the attacker need a password, what can they do afterwards) into one number from 0 to 10. Anything from 9.0 up is critical. Both php2shell flaws are 9.2 under version 4.0 of the scale. The leaked early reports said 10.0, which was wrong.

Where it matters in this story → · the authority ↗

### CWE

Common Weakness Enumeration: a catalogue of kinds of software weakness (the bug class), as opposed to CVE, which names one flaw.

Where a CVE names one specific flaw, a CWE names the type of mistake behind it, such as use-after-free (CWE-416). The php2shell records list five.

Where it matters in this story → · the authority ↗

## E

### End of life

A version the maintainers no longer fix. PHP 8.1 and older are end of life.

Software versions have a support window. After it ends, security fixes stop. PHP 8.1 and older are past theirs, so for organisations still on them php2shell is a migration project rather than an update.

Where it matters in this story →

### ENISA

The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity.

ENISA coordinates the EU's network of national response teams. Its advice on php2shell is one of the sixteen compared on the agencies page.

Where it matters in this story →

### Evidence vault

This site's private, encrypted store of every source it captured, each file hashed at the moment of capture.

Every page this site cites was saved, as served and as rendered, with a screenshot, into an encrypted vault. The pages themselves are not republished (they belong to their authors), but their fingerprints (hashes) are, so anyone can later check that nothing was changed.

Where it matters in this story →

### Exploit, exploitation

To exploit a flaw is to actually use it in an attack. Exploitation attempts are tries; a compromise is a success.

An exploit is the code or technique that turns a vulnerability into an attack. This site keeps three things apart: an exploit existing, attempts being seen (requests that look like the attack), and a confirmed compromise (a named system actually broken into). For php2shell, the first two are reported; the third has not been confirmed anywhere as of the latest capture.

Where it matters in this story →

## G

## U

### Unauthenticated

No login needed: anyone who can reach the website can try the attack.

### Use-after-free

A memory bug where a program keeps using memory after releasing it, so an attacker can control what is found there.

## V

### VEX

### Vulnerability

A flaw in software that an attacker can use to make it do something it should not.

## W

### WAF

Web application firewall: a filter in front of a website that blocks requests that look like attacks. A stopgap here, not a fix.

# What happened, does it affect me, and should I worry?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. No organisation has confirmed being broken into as of the latest evidence.

Read the site as Alex →

You do not need to know anything about computers to follow this. Below are the five things worth knowing, then the evidence behind them, folded away until you want it.

## What to decide or do
- **PHP is not on your phone or laptop.** It runs on the servers that build websites. This is a problem for the organisations that run those websites, and it is theirs to fix.
- **Nothing to install, nothing to change** on your own devices because of this. Be wary of any message that says otherwise and asks you to click or download something: scammers use headlines like this one.
- **If a website you use was down on 21 or 22 October, it was most likely a precaution.** Dutch government services such as DigiD were taken offline on purpose, as a precaution; that is a decision, not a sign of a break-in.
- **Nobody has confirmed being hacked through this yet.** Attackers have been trying, in large numbers, and that may change; this site will say so when the evidence does.
- **The big numbers in the headlines are not what they sound like.** 70% is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, not a share of the Internet that is broken. The numbers page explains each one.

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. No organisation has confirmed being broken into as of the latest evidence.

## What to decide or do
- **PHP is not on your phone or laptop.** It runs on the servers that build websites. This is a problem for the organisations that run those websites, and it is theirs to fix.
- **Nothing to install, nothing to change** on your own devices because of this. Be wary of any message that says otherwise and asks you to click or download something: scammers use headlines like this one.
- **If a website you use was down on 21 or 22 October, it was most likely a precaution.** Dutch government services such as DigiD were taken offline on purpose, as a precaution; that is a decision, not a sign of a break-in.
- **Nobody has confirmed being hacked through this yet.** Attackers have been trying, in large numbers, and that may change; this site will say so when the evidence does.
- **The big numbers in the headlines are not what they sound like.** 70% is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, not a share of the Internet that is broken. The numbers page explains each one.

## What to decide or do
- **PHP is not on your phone or laptop.** It runs on the servers that build websites. This is a problem for the organisations that run those websites, and it is theirs to fix.
- **Nothing to install, nothing to change** on your own devices because of this. Be wary of any message that says otherwise and asks you to click or download something: scammers use headlines like this one.

- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The BBC's list (parts of Wikipedia, Edinburgh council, French government services, the University of Geneva, the BBC itself) has not been captured from any of those organisations. Latvia's geo-blocking is the one documented case, from the agency itself.

# What happened, does it affect me, and should I worry?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. As of the evening of 22 October, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell.

Read the site as Alex →

You do not need to know anything about computers to follow this. Below are the five things worth knowing, then the evidence behind them, folded away until you want it.

## What to decide or do
- **PHP is not on your phone or laptop.** It runs on the servers that build websites. This is a problem for the organisations that run those websites, and it is theirs to fix.
- **Nothing to install, nothing to change** on your own devices because of this. Be wary of any message that says otherwise and asks you to click or download something: scammers use headlines like this one.
- **If a website you use was down on 21 or 22 October, it was most likely a precaution.** Dutch government services such as DigiD were taken offline on purpose, as a precaution; that is a decision, not a sign of a break-in.
- **Nobody has confirmed being hacked through this yet.** Attackers have been trying, in large numbers, and that may change; this site will say so when the evidence does.
- **The big numbers in the headlines are not what they sound like.** 70% is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, not a share of the Internet that is broken. The numbers page explains each one.

# What happened, does it affect me, and should I worry?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. As of the evening of 22 October, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell.

Read the site as Alex →

You do not need to know anything about computers to follow this. Below are the five things worth knowing, then the evidence behind them, folded away until you want it.

## What to decide or do
- **PHP is not on your phone or laptop.** It runs on the servers that build websites. This is a problem for the organisations that run those websites, and it is theirs to fix.
- **Nothing to install, nothing to change** on your own devices because of this. Be wary of any message that says otherwise and asks you to click or download something: scammers use headlines like this one.
- **If a website you use was down on 21 or 22 October, it was most likely a precaution.** Dutch government services such as DigiD were taken offline on purpose, as a precaution; that is a decision, not a sign of a break-in.
- **Nobody has confirmed being hacked through this yet.** Attackers have been trying, in large numbers, and that may change; this site will say so when the evidence does.
- **The big numbers in the headlines are not what they sound like.** 70% is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, not a share of the Internet that is broken. The numbers page explains each one.

PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

# What happened, does it affect me, and should I worry?

A
The answer in thirty seconds

Two serious holes were found in PHP, software that runs on the servers behind a large share of websites. They were fixed on 21 October 2026. Your phone and laptop are not the target: websites are, and it is the job of whoever runs them to update. Some sites were taken offline as a precaution. As of 16:05 UTC on 24 October, the latest capture in the evidence vault, no named organisation has said it was compromised through php2shell.

Read the site as Alex →

You do not need to know anything about computers to follow this. Below are the five things worth knowing, then the evidence behind them, folded away until you want it.

## What to decide or do
- **PHP is not on your phone or laptop.** It runs on the servers that build websites. This is a problem for the organisations that run those websites, and it is theirs to fix.
- **Nothing to install, nothing to change** on your own devices because of this. Be wary of any message that says otherwise and asks you to click or download something: scammers use headlines like this one.
- **If a website you use was down on 21 or 22 October, it was most likely a precaution.** Dutch government services such as DigiD were taken offline on purpose, as a precaution; that is a decision, not a sign of a break-in.
- **Nobody has confirmed being hacked through this yet.** Attackers have been trying, in large numbers, and that may change; this site will say so when the evidence does.
- **The big numbers in the headlines are not what they sound like.** 70% is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, not a share of the Internet that is broken. The numbers page explains each one.

## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.

The full set of claims is on every claim; the ordered steps for a vulnerable system are on if you run PHP. ## What is still open
- Who first leaked the CVE IDs on 20 October, and where. The PHP Foundation does not say; a PHP security team member points to an anonymous Hacker News post, and Notebookcheck and Nguoi Quan Sat repeat that account. No copy of the post is in the vault.
- Whether the deleted Calif video is the one now embedded on Calif's own write-up. Calif's page does not mention the leak.
- Whether any site was actually compromised before it was patched or taken offline. Every claim of exploitation so far is of attempts, probes or honeypot hits, and the named cases do not state php2shell as the cause. Authorities in Singapore and Luxembourg now ask operators to look for traces; the answer will come from those searches, if it comes.
- Which sites were really taken offline, and why. The list now draws on more captured reports (Germany's hospitals and hosts, Morocco, Romania, Japan), but most are press accounts; few come from the organisations themselves (the Dutch government, Latvia's agency, Weird Gloop, the Charité's spokesman as quoted). A community tracker counts 51 listed and 50 back.
- Whether the 8.5.12 fix is complete. A Fediverse report of a third bug or incomplete fix reached oss-security on 21 October; PHP reportedly told Canonical it is unrelated. On 23 October PHP published an informational advisory for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, in the session upload progress feature, reported by Cloudflare, SOCRadar and The Hacker News: it affects fully patched releases including 8.5.12, needs a rare session setting, will be fixed in the next regular release, and has session.upload_progress.enabled=0 as the mitigation; SOCRadar reports no exploitation and no severity score. PHP's advisory is not in the evidence vault, and whether this is the bug the Fediverse report described is not stated.
